title: The Global Economy and Economic Imperialism
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: In the 1830s Britain loved Chinese tea, silk, and porcelain, but China wanted little the British made and demanded payment in silver. British merchants reversed the silver drain by smuggling opium, an addictive narcotic grown in British-controlled India, into China by the ton.

The Chinese official Lin Zexu cracked down on the opium trade and destroyed huge stockpiles of British opium in 1839. Britain responded by going to war to defend its right to sell the drug, triggering the First Opium War.

Britain won the Opium War easily thanks to its industrial military power and forced China to sign a humiliating treaty: open ports to trade, cede Hong Kong, pay Britain's costs, and grant British merchants special privileges. These were the first of the 'unequal treaties.'

Economic imperialism is the use of economic power, pressure, and sometimes force to dominate other economies and bend them to the interests of the industrial powers, often without formally colonizing those regions.

Industrialization built, for the first time in history, a single integrated global economy, but a deeply unequal one in which the industrialized nations became the world's factories and bankers while the rest of the world supplied raw materials and bought finished goods.

The new global division of labor placed industrialized nations (Britain, Western Europe, the U.S., Japan) in the role of manufacturing goods and controlling finance and shipping, while colonized and dominated regions supplied raw materials and agricultural commodities and bought finished goods.

Economists describe the industrial-era world economy as a 'core' and 'periphery' relationship: an industrial core that manufactured goods and accumulated capital, and a periphery of regions reshaped to supply raw materials and cheap labor and left dependent.

Many regions became export-commodity economies, reshaped to produce one or a few products for the world market rather than diverse goods for themselves. This made them dependent on a single crop whose price they did not control and often reliant on imported food.

Whole territories were turned over to cash crops and extraction: rubber from the Congo, Brazil, and Malaya; cotton from Egypt and India; tea from India and Ceylon; sugar from the Caribbean; palm oil from West Africa; coffee from Brazil and Java; and copper, tin, diamonds, and gold from various colonies.

Local farmers who had grown food for their communities were often pushed into export crops by taxes that had to be paid in cash, by land seizures, or by direct compulsion. Cash-crop economies were frequently coerced, not freely chosen 'trade.'

Specialization in a single export commodity made regions vulnerable: a price crash or bad harvest could turn into famine, and wealth from the system flowed toward the industrial core rather than the regions supplying raw materials and labor.

After the Opium Wars, China signed 'unequal treaties' that opened treaty ports, controlled its tariffs, and granted foreigners extraterritoriality — meaning foreigners were not subject to Chinese law. China kept its flag but lost much of its economic independence.
China was never formally colonized, yet it was carved into spheres of influence and economically dominated, showing that economic imperialism could control a region without direct colonial rule.

Industrial powers and their banks lent enormous sums to governments in Egypt, the Ottoman Empire, and Latin America for railroads, canals, and modernization. When borrowers could not repay, lenders seized control of their finances or strategic assets, turning debt into a leash.
The Suez Canal, completed in 1869, linked the Mediterranean to the Red Sea and was a vital route to British India. Egypt borrowed heavily, including to build the canal.

Facing bankruptcy, Egypt's ruler sold its Suez Canal shares in 1875, and Britain bought them. European powers took control of Egyptian finances, and when a nationalist revolt erupted in 1882, Britain used it as a pretext to invade and occupy Egypt for decades.

Egypt's effort to modernize and resist domination through borrowing became the very mechanism of its domination: a loan to build the Suez Canal ultimately led to British occupation, illustrating economic imperialism's causal chain.

The new nations of Latin America won political independence in the early 1800s but fell into deep economic dependence on industrial powers, especially Britain and later the U.S., which dominated their trade, lent them money, owned their railroads, and bought their exports.

Latin America's situation — politically independent nations whose economies were nonetheless controlled from abroad — is sometimes called 'neo-colonialism' or informal empire, showing that imperialism's economic essence could be achieved through trade, investment, and debt rather than formal conquest.

Reasoning through a causal chain means establishing underlying conditions (an industrial global economy of European capital and dependent borrowers), identifying immediate triggers (Lin Zexu's opium destruction; Egypt's bankruptcy and 1882 revolt), linking causes so each leads to the next, and weighing which mattered most.

The dramatic gap between a rich 'global North' and a poorer 'global South' was created largely in the industrial century, a shift called the 'Great Divergence.' As late as 1750, Qing China and Mughal India were among the richest economies on earth.

Historians debate why some regions industrialized and grew rich while others stayed poor. One view stresses that industrialization concentrated capital and technology in a few places; another stresses that imperialism actively underdeveloped the rest by destroying local industries (e.g., British cloth devastating India's textile handicrafts), forcing dependent single-commodity economies, and extracting wealth.

Economic dependence created in the industrial era did not vanish when colonies won political independence; many newly independent nations remained tied to single-commodity exports and economically dominated, a condition critics labeled neo-colonialism and a root of modern global inequality debates.
